links.reason: Verse 1356 says the body perishes and fame stands for ever (பொன்றும் இவ்வுடல்; என்று நிற்கும் இரும்புகழ்), which agrees with the couplet's claim. It does not use the couplet as a reason or show who pays, and the verse is flagged uncertain.

Patikam line 3 (விஞ்சைக்கு இறைவன் மகள் வீணையில் தோற்றவாறும்) gives the outcome in advance, but it names no destiny. The father's 'பாற்படு காலம் வந்தால்' answered by the plan is the note's reading of a summary line.
22 sends Chandakarma into the city for the twins and 27 has the pair enter it, which is plot order. Nothing in 27 says the ascetic dress delivers them to the king.

The envoy takes the letter, is told to speak again himself (நீயே யுரை) and bows (கழலடி தொழுது), which is courtesy that fits the couplet's 'கடனறிந்து காலங்கருதி'. The verse shows no seating or gifts as a sequence that 'the couplet names', so the pair only illustrates.

The friend ranks lovers' union above even the state without birth and death (சாதலும் பிறத்தலும் இலாத தானமும் கோதென), which escalates the couplet's comparison with Vishnu's world. It is a real step, but it is a development of the couplet, not a limit on it.

261 has the plotter plan the kill while the king is sunk in pleasure, and 2610 has Vijayai retell it as the king 'swallowed by pleasure' (போகத்தால் விழுங்கப் பட்டு) who would not heed counsel (அமைச்சர் நுண்ணூல்). The survivor's account reads the same ruin as the king's own fault.

1574 is a hero's doubt about the world's pleasures at death (நன்றரோ நெஞ்சே) and 27 is the patikam summary of his renunciation. The claim that the doubt only keeps his restraint and that he marries again is from outside the two verses.

171 has the king vow to drive out the foes (நீக்குவன் என்றான்) and 172 has Udayanan's army destroy them, so a vow and its carrying out. But 172 ends with the king's return (நரபதியும் மீண்டனன்), and 'kept by the guest not the host' is the note's inference.

The poet blesses the king's sons (நோயிலர் ஆகநின் புதல்வர்) and leaves without anger, which fits the couplet. The poem names the fault only as a general rule about promising and refusing (lines 4-7), not as the king's fault, so the note overstates the 'plain naming'.
136 has the hidden men dig the tunnel and set the fire, and 139 has the king fall grieving at the signs. That is cause and plot sequence; the verses do not show his belief as the fire's aim.

The Kural describes a good fort that holds out and the poem shames the king who sits behind shut gates (திறவாது அடைத்த திண்ணிலைக் கதவின்) while elephants and babies suffer. The Kural makes no judgement of a king, so these are not incompatible claims, but the poem shows the moral cost of what the couplet praises.

2392 only orders elephants kept away and has the drum proclaim 'வாழ்க' for the seven days; it makes no claim about impermanence. The 'tension' is supplied by the quatrain, and the gains admit the epic leaves it 'unspoken'.

2884 asks whether the kin he cannot shake off are kin or enemies (சுற்றத்தாரோ பகைவரோ) and 2885 answers that in past and future births they were strangers (ஏதிலம்), so there is no kin. It is a rebirth argument, as the note says.
902 orders ornaments, drums, arches and golden pots, and 923 orders saffron, sandal and aloe smoke for the same wedding. This is plot sequence of two orders, and one adds nothing to the other.

Both praise wealth that serves many (பலர்க்கு ஆர்த்தி; ஊருணி நீர்நிறைந்தற்று). The 'perilous sea trade' and the claim that feeding many justifies the heavenly comparison are not in the Tamil, so this is an illustration.

103 lists engines that spit molten copper, balls, ghee, arrows and stones, and the Kural lists three ways of taking a fort. The irony that the city falls from within is from the plot elsewhere and the verse does not point to it.

Both give the reasoning that wealth is needed to feed kin (அழிபசி தீர்க்கும்; தம்நயந்து உறைவோர்த் தாங்கி). The fragment's speaker is unnamed, so 'treats it as needing no answer' rests on a reconstructed scene.

The verse itself calls her beauty மம்மர்நோய், a sickness of delusion, so the narrator does not offer it only as wonder. Both warn that adorned beauty bewilders, and the gains claims about a remedy and the strongest case are the note's own.

The paddy raises its head (தலை நிறுவி) when empty like base men's wealth and bows (இறைஞ்சிக் காய்த்த) when full like the learned, which matches the couplet's greatness that bows. The point that the two are stages of one thing is the note's reading of a simile, and the gains cannot be checked.

The word விருந்து is shared: Vipulan calls the challenger a guest (விருந்தாயினை எறி நீ) and the slain challenger goes to heaven (விசும்படைந்தான்). It turns the couplet's heaven for the host into heaven for the guest, but this rests on one word and 'the courtesy is not a figure of speech' overstates it.

The verse's நெருநல் ... இன்று frame matches the couplet's நெருநல் உளனொருவன் இன்றில்லை, so it instances the claim. 'By his own weapon' depends on whose discus செருநன் மறநேமி is, and the epic adds nothing the couplet lacks.

The link rests on the shared name Urandai/Uranthai. The epic verse lists the lord's drums, banners, waters and ghats and uses the name as his title, while the Akananuru poem uses it as a comparison for a rich house.

228 has the king ask whether a dream's nature is truth (கனவின் இயல் மெய் எனும்) and 267 has him say all she dreamt has come true, so the later verse reverses the earlier. Both are the king's words, so it is a reversal by events, not two claims in tension, and that the dismissal was feigned is not in the Tamil.

Both set a lamp or flame against darkness that stands for sin. In the quatrain it is the person's own tapas and the dark returns when the oil fails; in the verse it is the teacher's grace (அருளும் இன்னெனக்கு), and no limit is raised there.
1387 shows an unnamed youth in battle dress and 1390 has his kin name Kanaka Chitran as pressing into the fight. That the youth is the named hero is assumed, and the rest is plot order.

1611 praises the Jina who scorched Kama (காமனையுங் காய்ந்த) and 1488 says one woman's beauty makes her an enemy of Kama and others. These make no incompatible claim; 'the swing between desire and mastery' is a theme, not a conflict.

The Jina says that for a king renunciation is the excellent thing (மன்னவன் துறவெனத் துறத்தல் மாண்பு). The couplet is elliptical and contested, and 'hardest case' and 'renounce what you still hold' are not in either text.

Both say a product of a salty source is still prized (முந்நீர்ப் பிறந்த பவழம் உவர்க்கும் எனின்; களர்நிலத்துப் பிறந்த உப்பு). But the quatrain argues the worth of a learned man of low birth and the verse argues for a poem's faulty diction, and no dependence is shown.

2726 sets the monkey that lost the fruit beside Kattiyangaran (கைப்பழம் இழந்த மந்தி கட்டியங்காரன் ஒத்த) and the one that took it beside Civakan, and the note has this reversed. The link between the usurpation in 2614 and its reading as seizing and losing is real.

2052 has her resolve to win a boon from Anangan and 2058 has the king's friend speak a trick (பட்டிமை உரைத்தது) that she takes for the god's own voice. The prayer is answered by a human contrivance, as the note says.

314 has the deity take the hunchback Sanbagamalai's form and 358 has her say வஞ்சித்தேன் and return to her own place. The disguise and its admission are both in the Tamil; 'under the errand' is the one detail not shown.
The two are one antithesis: the bad deed nursed by anger (செற்றம் செவிலி) and the good deed by compassion (தயா எனும் செவிலி). Pairing them teaches only the contrast the two verses already state.

Patikam line 4 says only that he left her (கமழ் கோதையின் போயவாறும்), and 1505 shows it: he opens the door softly so that she should not know (அறிவுறா வகையின் ஒற்றி) and goes into the dark. The stealth is in the Tamil and absent from the summary.

142 has the mother offer the flour cock if he fears killing, and 144 says he shrinks even from making the shape of a creature because it is like killing (உயிர்க்கொலை போலும்) yet consents. The scruple shows the loophole is not clean to him; 'the cry at 146' is not checkable here.

The quatrain says kings under the umbrella were carried off and spoken of as dead, with none left over; 57 shows a king seized and does not show him dead. The rescue to come is not in 57, and the 'carried off' of the note misreads the quatrain's bier.

279 gives the dream and 282 has the sage say the bridegroom is coming and will rule the earth, so a dream and its reading. The reading is not the dream's fulfilment, and 282 does not name the lion and fish.

Both are the dry summer forest of the palai with sounding trees or pods (ஓமையே ... பறைந்தரோ; ஆடுகளப் பறையின் ஒலிப்ப), a stock landscape. The epic verse is not a woman's dread and the gains are not specific.

Acharakkovai 27 prescribes sipping three times, wiping and touching the face's parts with the fingers (முக்காற் குடித்துத் துடைத்து முகத்துறுப்பு விரலுறுத்தி), and 1302 does exactly this (மும்முறை குடித்து முக்கால் துடைத்த ... கைவிரல் உறுப்புத் தீட்டி). The sequence is the shared run of words.

310 has her alone in the burning ground not knowing how the child will grow, and 1913 has her call herself the base woman (கயத்தியேன்) who left him there. It is a later judgement on the earlier scene, not two incompatible claims, and the self-abasement may be address, not guilt.

Both burning grounds have owls (கூகை), jackals, ghouls or ghosts dancing, and pyre lamps (ஈம விளக்கு / ஈமம் விளக்காக). The Sangam poem has them greet the end of kings and the epic has them as the band for a prince's birth.

213 has the king reject talk of pleasures measured by penance (அது எனக்கு உரையல்), and 2728 has Civakan assert wives and sons as its fruit that the wind of sin will bring down. The doctrine returns, but the note leaves out that the first speaker refuses it.
1632 describes women's ornaments to please the king's eyes and makes no claim about the body. The quatrain's list of parts is not a rival claim on the same matter.

Both prefaces use a gem to excuse a faulty work: a gem-bundle valued with its cloth (மணிபொதி கிழி) and a gem that must be washed (கழுவாது விட்டால்). The difference between wrapping and washing is real, but it is a preface convention.

Both have the man tell his heart not to leave for wealth, one from the ruined hall on the road and one from the north wind and her bed (வடபுல வாடைக்குப் பிரிவோர் மடவர்). The poems are separate, so neither develops the other.
